title: Two kinds of p95
prompt: Five requests took 40, 10, 30, 1000 and 20 ms. This program computes their percentiles two ways, then the mean. What does it print? Type each line on its own line.
program:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

latencies = spark.createDataFrame([(ms,) for ms in [40, 10, 30, 1000, 20]], "latency_ms INT")

row = latencies.agg(
    F.percentile_approx("latency_ms", 0.5).alias("p50"),
    F.percentile_approx("latency_ms", 0.8).alias("p80"),
    F.percentile_approx("latency_ms", 0.95).alias("p95"),
    F.percentile("latency_ms", 0.5).alias("p50_i"),
    F.percentile("latency_ms", 0.8).alias("p80_i"),
    F.percentile("latency_ms", 0.95).alias("p95_i"),
    F.avg("latency_ms").alias("mean"),
).first()

print(row.p50, row.p80, row.p95)
print(round(row.p50_i, 1), round(row.p80_i, 1), round(row.p95_i, 1))  # doubles, rounded to 1 decimal
print(row.mean)
hints: Sort the latencies first. `percentile_approx` is exact on a group this small and returns a value from the list: the one at position `ceil(p × n)`.
`F.percentile` interpolates: it looks at position `p × (n - 1)`, counting from 0, and goes that far between the two neighbours. It returns a `double`.
The mean adds everything and divides by 5. One slow request moves it a long way.
explanation: Sorted, the latencies are 10, 20, 30, 40, 1000. By nearest rank, p50 is the 3rd value (ceil(2.5) = 3), 30; p80 is the 4th (ceil(4.0) = 4), 40; and p95 is the 5th (ceil(4.75) = 5), 1000. `percentile_approx` returns exactly those, as integers, because on fewer than about 10 000 values it is exact. `F.percentile` interpolates at position p × 4: 2.0 gives 30.0; 3.2 gives 40 + 0.2 × 960 = 232.0; 3.8 gives 40 + 0.8 × 960 = 808.0, a latency no request had. (The program rounds them to one decimal: as doubles they carry a tiny floating-point error.) The mean is 1100 / 5 = 220.0, higher than four of the five requests. Both percentile definitions are fine; mixing them gives one window two different p95s.
